nodes.title: Part 1: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 1. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is the official ITIL 4 definition of a 'service'?
flashcards.back: ITIL 4 defines a service as 'a means of enabling value co-creation by facilitating outcomes that customers want to achieve, without the customer having to manage specific costs and risks.' The other options describe a product, a procedure, and a physical deliverable — none of which capture the co-creation, outcome, cost, and risk elements that make ITIL's definition distinctive.

flashcards.front: How many guiding principles are defined in the ITIL 4 framework?
flashcards.back: ITIL 4 defines seven guiding principles: focus on value; start where you are; progress iteratively with feedback; collaborate and promote visibility; think and work holistically; keep it simple and practical; and optimize and automate. Five, six and nine are common distractors but do not match the official count.

flashcards.front: A service desk manager is deciding which improvement initiative to fund next. They want to make sure every activity contributes a meaningful result for stakeholders. Which ITIL 4 guiding principle most directly supports this decision?
flashcards.back: 'Focus on value' tells practitioners that every activity should directly or indirectly create value for stakeholders — exactly the lens this manager needs to choose between initiatives. 'Keep it simple and practical' avoids unnecessary steps but doesn't prioritize stakeholder value; 'Progress iteratively with feedback' is about delivery cadence; 'Optimize and automate' is about resource efficiency.

flashcards.front: Which of the following is one of the four dimensions of service management in ITIL 4?
flashcards.back: The four dimensions of service management are organizations and people, information and technology, partners and suppliers, and value streams and processes. The service value chain and continual improvement are components of the service value system, not dimensions. 'Service offering' is a service-relationship concept, not one of the four dimensions.

nodes.title: Part 2: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 2. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Which of the following is NOT a component of the ITIL 4 Service Value System (SVS)?
flashcards.back: The SVS components are guiding principles, governance, the service value chain, practices, and continual improvement. The service catalogue is an output managed by the service catalogue management practice, not a top-level SVS component. Guiding principles, governance and practices are all explicitly part of the SVS.

flashcards.front: Within the ITIL 4 service value chain, which activity is responsible for providing a good understanding of stakeholder needs, transparency, and continual engagement and relationships?
flashcards.back: 'Engage' is the value-chain activity that handles all interactions with stakeholders to capture needs, set expectations and maintain relationships. 'Plan' establishes vision and direction, 'Improve' targets continual improvement of products and practices, and 'Deliver and support' covers operating services. The six activities are plan, improve, engage, design and transition, obtain/build, and deliver and support.

flashcards.front: A user reports that the email service is unavailable. The service desk records a ticket and the team immediately starts work to restore the service. Which ITIL 4 practice is being applied?
flashcards.back: Restoring a degraded or interrupted service as quickly as possible is the purpose of incident management. Problem management would investigate the underlying cause once service is restored; change enablement governs changes to the environment; service request management handles routine user requests such as access or new equipment — none of which is the immediate outage response described here.

flashcards.front: Which statement best describes a 'standard change' in ITIL 4 change enablement?
flashcards.back: Standard changes are low-risk, well-understood, and pre-authorized — for example, a routine password reset or a documented patch rollout. Emergency changes are urgent fixes; normal changes go through the regular assessment and authorization workflow (often a CAB); a never-performed-before change is the opposite of standard and would be treated as a normal or even high-risk change.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the ITIL 4 Service Value System (SVS)?
choices: Service catalogue
Guiding principles
Governance
Practices
questions.explanation: The SVS components are guiding principles, governance, the service value chain, practices, and continual improvement. The service catalogue is an output managed by the service catalogue management practice, not a top-level SVS component. Guiding principles, governance and practices are all explicitly part of the SVS.

questions.q: Within the ITIL 4 service value chain, which activity is responsible for providing a good understanding of stakeholder needs, transparency, and continual engagement and relationships?
choices: Improve
Engage
Plan
Deliver and support
questions.explanation: 'Engage' is the value-chain activity that handles all interactions with stakeholders to capture needs, set expectations and maintain relationships. 'Plan' establishes vision and direction, 'Improve' targets continual improvement of products and practices, and 'Deliver and support' covers operating services. The six activities are plan, improve, engage, design and transition, obtain/build, and deliver and support.

questions.q: A user reports that the email service is unavailable. The service desk records a ticket and the team immediately starts work to restore the service. Which ITIL 4 practice is being applied?
choices: Problem management (find and remove the underlying cause of incidents)
Change enablement (assess, authorize and schedule changes)
Incident management (restore normal service operation as quickly as possible)
Service request management (handle predefined, user-initiated requests)
questions.explanation: Restoring a degraded or interrupted service as quickly as possible is the purpose of incident management. Problem management would investigate the underlying cause once service is restored; change enablement governs changes to the environment; service request management handles routine user requests such as access or new equipment — none of which is the immediate outage response described here.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a 'standard change' in ITIL 4 change enablement?
choices: A change that must be implemented as soon as possible to resolve a major incident or restore critical service
A change that requires authorization from the change advisory board on each occurrence before it can proceed
A change that has never been performed before and carries significant unknown risk to the live environment
A low-risk, pre-authorized change that follows a defined procedure or work instruction whenever it is performed
questions.explanation: Standard changes are low-risk, well-understood, and pre-authorized — for example, a routine password reset or a documented patch rollout. Emergency changes are urgent fixes; normal changes go through the regular assessment and authorization workflow (often a CAB); a never-performed-before change is the opposite of standard and would be treated as a normal or even high-risk change.

nodes.title: Part 3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 3. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is the FIRST step of the ITIL 4 continual improvement model?
flashcards.back: The continual improvement model starts with 'What is the vision?' to align any improvement effort with the wider business vision before doing anything else. 'Where are we now?' is the baseline assessment that follows; 'Where do we want to be?' defines measurable targets; and 'How do we get there?' plans the actions. The full sequence is vision → baseline → targets → plan → take action → did we get there? → keep the momentum going.

flashcards.front: Which ITIL 4 practice is responsible for handling predefined, user-initiated requests such as access to an application or provision of a laptop?
flashcards.back: Service request management handles all predefined, user-initiated requests — typically routine, low-risk, and fulfilled against a documented workflow. The service desk is the entry point that may capture the request but is a separate practice; problem management investigates root causes of incidents; service level management negotiates and monitors service-level targets.

flashcards.front: A new collaboration platform lets employees message colleagues (the feature they need) and is guaranteed to be available 99.9% of the time. The 99.9% availability target represents which aspect of the service?
flashcards.back: Warranty answers 'how' a service performs — its fitness for use, expressed through targets such as availability, capacity, security and continuity. Utility answers 'what' the service does (fitness for purpose) — here, enabling messaging. Outcomes are the results customers achieve; cost is what they pay. A service must deliver both utility and warranty to create value.

flashcards.front: What is the primary purpose of the ITIL 4 service desk practice?
flashcards.back: The service desk's primary purpose is to be the single point of contact between the service provider and its users — capturing incident reports and service requests and routing them appropriately. The first option describes incident management; the second describes change enablement; the third describes service level management.

questions.q: What is the FIRST step of the ITIL 4 continual improvement model?
choices: What is the vision?
Where are we now?
Where do we want to be?
How do we get there?
questions.explanation: The continual improvement model starts with 'What is the vision?' to align any improvement effort with the wider business vision before doing anything else. 'Where are we now?' is the baseline assessment that follows; 'Where do we want to be?' defines measurable targets; and 'How do we get there?' plans the actions. The full sequence is vision → baseline → targets → plan → take action → did we get there? → keep the momentum going.

questions.q: Which ITIL 4 practice is responsible for handling predefined, user-initiated requests such as access to an application or provision of a laptop?
choices: Service desk
Service request management
Problem management
Service level management
questions.explanation: Service request management handles all predefined, user-initiated requests — typically routine, low-risk, and fulfilled against a documented workflow. The service desk is the entry point that may capture the request but is a separate practice; problem management investigates root causes of incidents; service level management negotiates and monitors service-level targets.

questions.q: A new collaboration platform lets employees message colleagues (the feature they need) and is guaranteed to be available 99.9% of the time. The 99.9% availability target represents which aspect of the service?
choices: Utility — what the service does
Outcome — the result the customer is enabled to achieve
Warranty — assurance that the service will meet agreed requirements (fitness for use)
Cost — the resources the consumer must spend on the service
questions.explanation: Warranty answers 'how' a service performs — its fitness for use, expressed through targets such as availability, capacity, security and continuity. Utility answers 'what' the service does (fitness for purpose) — here, enabling messaging. Outcomes are the results customers achieve; cost is what they pay. A service must deliver both utility and warranty to create value.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of the ITIL 4 service desk practice?
choices: To minimize the negative impact of incidents by restoring normal service operation as quickly as possible
To plan, schedule and authorize all changes to the live IT environment so that risk is controlled
To set clear business-based service-level targets and monitor and report delivery against them
To capture demand for incident resolution and service requests, acting as the entry point and single point of contact for users
questions.explanation: The service desk's primary purpose is to be the single point of contact between the service provider and its users — capturing incident reports and service requests and routing them appropriately. The first option describes incident management; the second describes change enablement; the third describes service level management.
